plan.summary: Budget leans to the two home publishers whose notes name the actual purchase moment \u2014 Northbed's home cross-sell and Hearthstone's gifting/new-home events \u2014 with smaller tests on gift-season socks (Heartfoot), clean-claim grocery (Pantrygood) and self-care bookings (Studiogrid); everything else is demographic overlap only and stays excluded.

recommended.name: Northbed
recommended.tier_reason: The score treated this as generic home overlap, but the record shows a direct purchase-moment link the tag map underweighted: someone just outfitting a bedroom or bath with bedding from a design-led brand is exactly who adds a decorative candle, and the notes confirm the cross-sell behaviour.
recommended.rationale: Notes say "High cross-sell with home and wellness" for "Design-conscious" buyers, and a $40 candle against a $164 bedding basket is an easy add-on to a room someone is already styling.

evidence.quote: Design-conscious urban/suburban buyers. High cross-sell with home and wellness

recommended.risk: 3.6M impressions is the smallest reach among the strong fits, so volume will be capped even at a good conversion rate.

recommended.name: Hearthstone Goods
recommended.tier_reason: Category scoring only found a weak kitchen\u2248home_decor link, but the notes name the exact occasion this advertiser sells into (gifting and new-home events) and a non-toxic sensibility that matches the "no synthetic fragrances" claim.
recommended.rationale: Notes say "Gifting and new-home life events drive purchase" for "Sustainability-motivated" buyers, and a $40 hand-poured soy candle is a natural gift or housewarming add-on to a $198 cookware order.

evidence.quote: Sustainability-motivated kitchen buyers. Gifting and new-home life events drive purchase

recommended.risk: 2.8M impressions limits scale, and cookware gifting peaks seasonally.

test.name: Heartfoot
test.tier_reason: Scored off-category on apparel, but the publisher's own gifting subcategory and seasonal gift uplift put this shopper in a gift-buying mindset, which is the occasion this brand says drives most of its sales.
test.rationale: Notes cite "Strong gifting season uplift (Nov-Dec)" alongside a "gifting" subcategory, so a $40 gift candle sits naturally next to a $52 gift-sock basket; worth measuring whether the gift intent carries outside Q4.

evidence.quote: Strong gifting season uplift (Nov-Dec). Audience responds to social-good messaging

test.risk: Gift intent may be concentrated in Nov-Dec, and the audience responds to social-good messaging rather than the craft/natural story this brand tells.

test.name: Pantrygood
test.tier_reason: Values signal was scored at 33 on clean_ingredients alone, but the notes describe an audience that buys specifically on the claims this brand leads with (natural, no synthetics), which is a testable hypothesis rather than an off-category dismissal.
test.rationale: Notes say shoppers are "Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims" \u2014 the same framing as "Natural soy wax, no synthetic fragrances" \u2014 at a $86 basket that makes a $40 candle affordable.

evidence.quote: Values-driven shoppers. Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

test.risk: The link is values-based, not purchase-based: nothing in a pantry restock order suggests home decor is on this shopper's mind.

test.name: Studiogrid
test.tier_reason: Excluded as off-category, but the self-care purchase moment is a real hypothesis for a candle: the notes show users actively spending on relaxation, and the $42 basket sits right at the candle's price point.
test.rationale: Notes say users are "actively spending on self-care" via spa and yoga bookings, so an at-home-ritual candle is a plausible next purchase at a matched $42 ticket \u2014 test whether a service booking converts to a physical goods buy.

evidence.quote: Appointment-based booking. Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

test.risk: Booking a class is not a shopping mindset, and this brand's own occasion mix skews to gifting rather than self-treat.

experiment.graduate_rule: After 14 days, move a test publisher to core if its CPA is at or below target; cut any placement above max CPA.
experiment.notes: Creatives rotate evenly until each has enough conversions to compare.

assumptions: Assumed a premium price point with a first order around $40, since no prices were given.
Assumed a broad adult audience with no gender skew.
Assumed one-time purchases rather than a candle subscription.
Allowable CPA is 30% of first order value (one time); replace with real margin and LTV.
warnings: The ads for The Affluent Classic, The Gen Z Aesthete won't run: no placement's shoppers fit those personas.
Target CPA is based on an assumed order value. Confirm price before launch.

launch_summary.summary: Most of the budget — $8,500, or 85% — goes to two home publishers, Northbed and Hearthstone Goods, whose shoppers are already mid home or gifting purchase. The remaining $1,500 splits evenly across three tests: Heartfoot for gift-season socks, Pantrygood for clean-ingredient grocery shoppers, and Studiogrid for self-care bookings, each asking whether gift intent, values alignment or a service booking carries over to a candle. Paying $12.00 per new customer, with results judged at 14 days.
uncertainties: The $40 first order value is assumed, and the $12.00 target cost per new customer is built directly on it, so a different price changes the whole economics.
Ads for The Affluent Classic and The Gen Z Aesthete won't run at all, because no placement's shoppers fit those personas.
The plan assumes one-time purchases rather than a subscription, which is why the first order alone has to pay back acquisition.
questions: What does a first order actually cost, and what is the margin on it?
Do buyers repeat or subscribe, or is this genuinely one-time?
Is the audience broad adult with no gender skew, as assumed?
